notes.scenario_families: The three highway modes this repository's CARLA port realizes (carla_highway/scenarios.py), mapped onto the harness's family names: cut_in -> cutin, lane_change -> hard_brake, overtake -> overtake. The second is the one to check rather than trust: the port's mode is named for what the slow lead does and the family for what the ego must decide, and they are the same scenario described from the two ends -- IMPLEMENTATION.md section 5.3's 'slow lead constrains the ego lane while an adjacent vehicle constrains the alternative lane'. The three intersection families are the sibling port's (third_party/orchestration) and a request for one of them is answered with an explicit failure rather than a substituted scenario.
notes.orchestration: Only `cutin` actually orchestrates: the role is CAST from the live scene and the holder is re-planned toward an ego-relative pin every 0.1 s, with recasting when the holder becomes geometrically hopeless. `hard_brake` and `overtake` turn casting off on purpose (carla_highway/scenarios.py :: ModeSpec) because cast roles or yields would change the very timings those scenarios are tuned around, so on those two this method executes an authored scenario rather than orchestrating one. That distinction matters for any comparison against a scripted baseline and is recorded per run in `orchestration.casting`.
notes.ttc_target: Absolute for `cutin` -- the cut-in pin's `along` is solved from the target and the ego's free-flow speed, so the ego's projected time to the merge point is the target by construction. An OFFSET on the conflict actor's spawn station for the two non-casting modes, where there is no plan to re-solve: the authored conflict timing is the baseline and the delivered time-to-conflict tracks the request with that baseline added. Which of the two applied is in every run's notes.
notes.observation_spaces: The port owns the CARLA world and describes the scene as object-centric state plus a BEV raster the policy's own renderer produces. It also attaches whatever sensor rig a policy declares through sensors() -- cameras, LiDAR and radar (carla_port/carla_sensors.py, shared with the sibling port) -- so a camera/LiDAR policy runs here too; a policy that declares no rig gets state only, exactly as before.
notes.action_spaces: The ego is actuated from a control (carla_port/actuation.py, shared with the sibling port so both actuate one control law). A policy declaring 'waypoints' is accepted and run through the control its own controllers return alongside them; 'trajectory' is not accepted.
notes.policies: The analytic IDM family (idm, idm_assertive, idm_conservative) is realized natively by binding the request onto carla_highway/highway_ego.py's own IDM constants, including IDM_V0_CUTIN so a requested desired speed applies to all three modes. Any other ego_policy_v1 policy is loaded from its own repository through build_policy(request) / policy.act(observation).
notes.trace: Per-tick canonical trace (states.jsonl + scene.json) on by default, written by carla_highway/trace_recording.py, so the harness's metrics package can evaluate scenario success from the realized trajectory rather than from this method's self-report. The ego's declared reference path is the lane it STARTED in, not the trajectory it drove: a lane change is what two of these three families are about, and a reference recovered from the driven path would fold the manoeuvre into the baseline.
notes.environment: CARLA 0.9.16 in synchronous mode, pygame (the script layer imports it), and -- for an external policy -- that policy's own inference stack in the same interpreter. The project's carla-ubuntu20-plant2 Apptainer image provides all three. `python3 -m carla_highway.validate --xodr-dir <OpenDrive>` checks the road fit against real Town geometry with no server: 121 checks.
